segments.t: Still in Vika's apartment, Max stumbles through an awkward argument about whether they have any future left together. When Vika tells him to leave, Max admits he does not want to go, and their heated confrontation suddenly turns into a passionate reconciliation.
И все.
Значит, хорошо?
Ну, то, что ты с ним.
Что хорошо?
Ну, в смысле, не с ним, а я.
Черт, как все запуталось.
Вика, что нам делать?
Нет никаких нас.
Есть я и ты.
Я хочу, чтобы ты ушел.
Подожди, я не хочу, чтобы не уходил.
Если я скажу нет, ты уйдешь?
Я серьезно.

'Well, the fact that you are with him.' Nastya brings out the contrast between 'come on' and 'then' in a few short words.

'What is good about it?' Notice how Russian expresses 'what' and 'fine' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Vika answers right away.

'Well, I mean not with him, but me.' In Russian, the idea of 'come on' flows naturally into 'I' without extra filler words.

'Damn, how complicated everything has become.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'darn' before landing on 'get confused'.

'Vika, what should we do?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'Vika' and finishing on 'what is one to do'. Vika answers right away.
Нет никаких нас.
'There is no 'us'.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'there is no' and finishing on 'us'.

'There is only you and me.' Nastya anchors the line on 'there is', while 'you' completes the thought.
Я хочу, чтобы ты ушел.
'I want you to leave.' The meaning hinges on 'I' working together with 'left' in spoken Russian. Vika answers right away.
Подожди, я не хочу, чтобы не уходил.
'Wait, I do not want to leave.' In Russian, the idea of 'wait' flows naturally into 'to leave' without extra filler words.
Если я скажу нет, ты уйдешь?
'If I say no, will you leave?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'if' before landing on 'you'll leave'.
Я серьезно.
